A 45-year-old woman presents to the acute care clinic with sudden-onset, severe, continuous rotational vertigo that began 2 days ago. She has persistent nausea and has vomited several times. She prefers lying completely still in bed with her eyes closed. She explicitly has no hearing loss, tinnitus, or aural fullness. Physical examination reveals horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating toward the left that is suppressed by visual fixation. Otoscopy, cranial nerve examination, and cerebellar testing are normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of acute, continuous, prolonged rotational vertigo lasting days (48–72 hours) with prominent autonomic symptoms (nausea, vomiting) and unilateral peripheral horizontal nystagmus, in the complete absence of auditory or neurological deficits, is the hallmark of Vestibular Neuritis (Neuronitis).

Pathogenesis: Vestibular neuritis is an acute inflammatory neuropathy typically attributed to post-viral or viral reactivation (often Herpes Simplex Virus type 1) selectively affecting the vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), most commonly the superior vestibular nerve. Because the cochlear nerve and labyrinthine hair cells are spared, hearing is entirely normal. In contrast, if acute continuous vertigo is accompanied by acute unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, the diagnosis is acute labyrinthitis.

High-Yield: Acute Prolonged Vertigo Rule: Continuous vertigo for days + Normal Hearing = Vestibular Neuritis. Continuous vertigo for days + Hearing Loss = Acute Labyrinthitis.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Always perform the HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) in acute continuous vertigo to rule out a cerebellar stroke mimicking vestibular neuritis. A normal head impulse test (no catch-up saccade) in acute vertigo strongly suggests a central stroke!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: BPPV causes transient paroxysms of vertigo lasting seconds provoked by positional head changes, not continuous unremitting vertigo lasting 2 days.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Ménière's disease presents with episodic vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus, and ear fullness.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: The clinical scenario of acute, continuous, prolonged rotational vertigo lasting days (48–72 hours) with prominent autonomic symptoms (nausea, vomiting) and unilateral peripheral horizontal nystagmus, in the complete absence of auditory or neurological deficits, is the hallmark of Vestibular Neuritis (Neuronitis).
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) causes progressive asymmetric SNHL, tinnitus, and mild dysequilibrium, not acute continuous violent vertigo.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose vestibular neuritis based on acute continuous vertigo lasting days with nausea/vomiting and completely intact hearing.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female presents with acute vestibular neuritis of 2 days' duration with severe nausea and continuous vertigo.

What is the most appropriate management strategy?
questions.explanation:
The evidence-based treatment for acute Vestibular Neuritis consists of supportive symptomatic care combined with a tapering course of systemic corticosteroids.

1. Corticosteroids: Oral methylprednisolone or prednisone significantly accelerates peripheral vestibular recovery and reduces long-term caloric asymmetry when initiated within the first few days of onset.
2. Supportive Care: Short-term vestibular suppressants (e.g., dimenhydrinate, meclizine, diazepam) and antiemetics (ondansetron, promethazine) are used strictly for the first 24 to 48 hours to manage disabling nausea and vomiting.
3. Vestibular Rehabilitation: Vestibular suppressants must be discontinued after 48 hours because prolonged use delays central vestibular compensation. Early physical mobilization and vestibular rehabilitation exercises are encouraged to promote central recovery.

High-Yield: Vestibular Neuritis Management: 1) Short-term vestibular suppressants (< 48 hours only); 2) Oral steroids to hasten peripheral nerve recovery; 3) Early ambulation and Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT) for central compensation.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Never continue vestibular suppressants (antihistamines, benzodiazepines) long-term in vestibular neuritis. They inhibit the brainstem's ability to achieve central vestibular compensation!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: The Dix-Hallpike test is used to diagnose BPPV and will only cause distress without diagnostic utility in acute continuous neuritis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: The evidence-based treatment for acute Vestibular Neuritis consists of supportive symptomatic care combined with a tapering course of systemic corticosteroids.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Vestibular neurectomy is an invasive destructive surgical procedure reserved as a last resort for intractable Ménière's disease.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: The Epley maneuver is the repositioning treatment for BPPV; it has no role in vestibular neuritis.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect: Antivirals (acyclovir/valacyclovir) have shown no efficacy in improving vestibular recovery over steroids alone in clinical trials.

questions.educationalObjective: Select supportive therapy with short-term antiemetics/suppressants and systemic corticosteroids as the management of choice for acute vestibular neuritis.

questions.question:
On an axial high-resolution computed tomography (CT) scan of the petrous temporal bone at the level of the epitympanum and vestibule, pointer number 3 designates a delicate bony canal traveling anterolaterally from the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus toward the geniculate ganglion area.

What anatomical structure does number 3 represent?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Axial Temporal Bone CT: Shows pointer number 3 directed at the bony canal of the labyrinthine segment of the facial nerve, extending from the fundus of the internal auditory canal anterolaterally to the geniculate ganglion.
questions.explanation:
On this axial temporal bone CT, pointer number 3 indicates the bony canal of the facial nerve (CN VII) (specifically its labyrinthine segment leading to the first genu and geniculate ganglion).

The intratemporal course of the facial nerve is divided into three primary segments:
1. Labyrinthine segment (labeled 3): Runs anterolaterally from the fundus of the IAC above the cochlea to the geniculate ganglion. It is the narrowest (0.68 mm) and shortest (~3–4 mm) portion of the canal, making it the most susceptible site for entrapment and ischemia in Bell's palsy.

2. Tympanic (horizontal) segment: Runs along the medial wall of the middle ear above the oval window.
3. Mastoid (vertical) segment: Descends from the second genu down to the stylomastoid foramen.

High-Yield: Facial Nerve Intratemporal Segments: 1) Labyrinthine (shortest & narrowest, site of Bell's palsy compression); 2) Tympanic / Horizontal (most commonly dehiscent, vulnerable during stapes surgery); 3) Mastoid / Vertical (gives off nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: The labyrinthine segment of the facial nerve is the narrowest portion of the entire fallopian canal (< 0.7 mm wide).

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: The lateral semicircular canal is labeled number 7 (posteriorly located horizontal ring).
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: The cochlea is the large snail-shaped cavity located anteromedially in the petrous bone.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: On this axial temporal bone CT, pointer number 3 indicates the bony canal of the facial nerve (CN VII) (specifically its labyrinthine segment leading to the first genu and geniculate ganglion).
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: The utricle is located inside the fluid-filled vestibule medial to the lateral semicircular canal.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the facial nerve canal (labyrinthine segment) on axial temporal bone CT.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of painless, progressive left-sided hearing loss and persistent, malodorous, scanty otorrhea unresponsive to multiple courses of topical antibiotic drops. High-magnification otoscopic examination (shown in the attached image) reveals a deep retraction pocket in the pars flaccida (attic) of the tympanic membrane with bone erosion of the scutum, filled with pearly-white flaky keratin debris and granulation tissue.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Otoscopy Image: Displays an attic retraction pocket containing pearly-white keratinaceous lamellae, crusting, and granulation tissue eroding the lateral attic wall (scutum), pathognomonic for a primary acquired cholesteatoma.

options.C: Chronic otitis media with squamous debris (cholesteatoma)

questions.explanation:
The combination of chronic, foul-smelling otorrhea, progressive conductive hearing loss, and otoscopic visualization of an attic retraction pocket containing pearly-white squamous keratin debris and granulations is pathognomonic for Cholesteatoma (chronic otitis media with squamous debris).

Pathogenesis: A primary acquired cholesteatoma develops when chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction creates sustained negative middle ear pressure, sucking the weak, non-cartilaginous pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) into the attic (epitympanum). Desquamated keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium accumulates within this expanding retraction pocket. Osteoclasts and local inflammatory cytokines (collagenases, TNF-alpha) produce progressive enzymatic bone erosion, destroying the ossicular chain (incus long process first), scutum, tegmen tympani (skull base), facial nerve canal, and lateral semicircular canal. Definitive treatment is surgical (tympanomastoidectomy).

High-Yield: Cholesteatoma Core Facts: Hallmark = Attic crust/retraction with foul-smelling discharge and white keratin debris. Complication = Bone erosion leading to ossicular destruction, facial nerve palsy, labyrinthine fistula, or brain abscess. Definitive therapy = Surgical excision (mastoidectomy).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Never treat an attic crust with repeated antibiotic drops alone. An attic crust with foul odor is a cholesteatoma until proven otherwise and requires immediate CT imaging and otolaryngology surgical referral.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Chronic otitis externa causes itching, canal thickening, and scaling confined to the external canal skin, without attic retraction pockets or middle ear keratin flakes.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Otitis media with effusion presents with an intact amber/yellow eardrum and fluid/air bubbles without discharge or squamous keratin debris.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: The combination of chronic, foul-smelling otorrhea, progressive conductive hearing loss, and otoscopic visualization of an attic retraction pocket containing pearly-white squamous keratin debris and granulations is pathognomonic for Cholesteatoma (chronic otitis media with squamous debris).
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Acute otitis media is an acute painful bacterial infection with fever, severe otalgia, and a bulging red tympanic membrane.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize chronic otitis media with squamous debris (cholesteatoma) based on chronic malodorous otorrhea and an attic retraction pocket containing keratin squames.

questions.question:
A clinical photograph depicts an automated handheld acoustic device with a soft probe tip placed in the external auditory canal of a sleeping newborn infant. The device is being used as part of universal neonatal sensory screening programs before discharge from the maternity ward.

What is the name of this screening device?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Clinical Photograph: Displays an infant undergoing hearing screening using a handheld automated Otoacoustic Emission (OAE) screening unit equipped with an ear-canal probe.
questions.explanation:
The device shown is an automated Otoacoustic Emission (OAE) screening device, which is one of the two primary screening modalities (alongside Automated Auditory Brainstem Response [AABR]) utilized worldwide in Universal Newborn Hearing Screening (UNHS) protocols.

OAE testing is fast (takes ~1–2 minutes per ear), objective, non-invasive, and painless. It does not require active behavioral participation from the infant and can be performed while the infant is naturally resting or sleeping. A probe containing a miniature speaker and sensitive microphone is inserted into the ear canal to introduce acoustic clicks or tone bursts and detect the cochlea's low-intensity acoustic response.

High-Yield: Newborn Hearing Screening Modalities: 1) OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions) = tests pre-neural outer hair cell function; 2) AABR (Automated Auditory Brainstem Response) = tests the complete auditory pathway up to the brainstem (detects auditory neuropathy). If a baby fails initial OAE, follow-up with AABR is mandatory.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: OAE only tests up to the outer hair cells of the cochlea! It CANNOT detect auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder or retrocochlear lesions. For infants in the neonatal ICU (NICU) at risk for auditory neuropathy, AABR is the required screening tool.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: The device shown is an automated Otoacoustic Emission (OAE) screening device, which is one of the two primary screening modalities (alongside Automated Auditory Brainstem Response [AABR]) utilized worldwide in Universal Newborn Hearing Screening (UNHS) protocols.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Pure Tone Audiometry requires voluntary behavioral responses (raising a hand or pressing a button) and cannot be used in infants.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: A pneumatic otoscope is a manual handheld visual tool used to assess tympanic membrane mobility.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: An impedance tympanometer measures middle ear pressure and compliance, not cochlear hair cell sound generation.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Otoacoustic Emission (OAE) device as a primary objective screening tool used in universal newborn hearing assessment.

questions.question:
Regarding the biophysical mechanism of the handheld newborn hearing screening device (Otoacoustic Emission):

How does this device work to evaluate auditory integrity?

options.A: Sound stimulates the cochlea, and the outer hair cells vibrate (electromotility)
options.B: Electrodes record electrical potentials generated along the brainstem auditory nuclei
options.C: Air pressure changes measure the acoustic impedance of the tympanic membrane
options.D: The infant's head turn toward an acoustic source is visually observed

questions.explanation:
Otoacoustic Emissions (OAEs) are low-intensity acoustic sounds generated within the normal cochlea by the active mechanical vibration (electromotility) of the outer hair cells (OHCs) in response to auditory stimulation.

Biophysical Principle: The OAE probe speaker delivers acoustic click stimuli into the ear canal. The sound travels through the ossicular chain into the cochlea, stimulating the basilar membrane. The outer hair cells contain the voltage-sensitive motor protein prestin. When depolarized, prestin contracts and expands the cell bodies of the outer hair cells at acoustic frequencies. This active mechanical amplification generates backward-traveling acoustic energy ('cochlear echoes') that travels out through the stapes, tympanic membrane, and ear canal, where a sensitive microphone in the probe records the emission. Presence of an OAE confirms normal outer hair cell function and hearing thresholds better than 25–30 dB HL.

High-Yield: OAE Mechanism: Outer hair cells act as biological acoustic amplifiers via prestin-mediated electromotility. Inner hair cells transduce sound into neural spikes (95% of afferents). Outer hair cells generate the OAE response.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: A patient with Auditory Neuropathy Spectrum Disorder will have NORMAL OAEs (normal outer hair cells) but ABSENT Auditory Brainstem Responses (ABR) and severe hearing impairment.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: Otoacoustic Emissions (OAEs) are low-intensity acoustic sounds generated within the normal cochlea by the active mechanical vibration (electromotility) of the outer hair cells (OHCs) in response to auditory stimulation.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Recording electrical auditory brainstem potentials using scalp electrodes describes Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR/BAER), not OAE.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Measuring impedance and compliance changes under pneumatic pressure describes acoustic immittance/ tympanometry.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Observing head turning toward sound describes Visual Reinforcement Audiometry (VRA), used in older infants (6–24 months).

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the biophysical basis of Otoacoustic Emissions as sound generated by the active electromotility of outer hair cells in the cochlea. USMLE Step 2 CK Integration • Otolaryngology Core Clinical Curriculum

questions.question:
A 38-year-old male with a documented history of cystic fibrosis presents with a 1-year history of persistent bilateral nasal obstruction, purulent rhinorrhea, dull facial pressure across the cheeks, and troublesome post-nasal drip. Anterior rhinoscopy and coronal CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrate bilateral extensive opacification of the ethmoid and maxillary sinuses with mucosal thickening and bilateral nasal polyps.

What is the diagnosis?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Coronal CT and Endoscopic View: CT shows diffuse soft-tissue opacification of bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinuses with sinonasal polyposis without gross bone erosion; endoscopy reveals multiple pale, gelatinous polyps prolapsing from the middle meatus.
questions.explanation:
The patient meets the international consensus diagnostic criteria for Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS): persistent inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses lasting ≥ 12 weeks, accompanied by at least two cardinal symptoms (nasal obstruction, facial pain/pressure, purulent drainage, or hyposmia/anosmia) and documented mucosal inflammation on endoscopy or sinus CT.

In patients with cystic fibrosis (CF), defective CFTR chloride channels lead to dehydrated, hyperviscous mucus, impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic bacterial colonization, and persistent sinonasal inflammation. Over 90% of adults with cystic fibrosis have radiographic evidence of chronic pansinusitis, and 30–50% develop extensive bilateral sinonasal polyposis (CRSwNP).

High-Yield: Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS) requires ≥ 12 consecutive weeks of symptoms PLUS objective endoscopic or CT confirmation of sinonasal inflammation. In children, any presentation of bilateral nasal polyps MUST prompt sweat chloride testing or CFTR genetic testing to exclude cystic fibrosis.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Nasal polyps in a child under 12 years are considered cystic fibrosis until proven otherwise!

optionExplanations.A: Correct: The patient meets the international consensus diagnostic criteria for Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS): persistent inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses lasting ≥ 12 weeks, accompanied by at least two cardinal symptoms (nasal obstruction, facial pain/pressure, purulent drainage, or hyposmia/anosmia) and documented mucosal inflammation on endoscopy or sinus CT.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) typically occurs in young immunocompetent atopic individuals with marked serum IgE elevation, showing expansile hyperdense (calcified) allergic mucin on CT.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Acute rhinosinusitis is defined as sudden-onset symptoms lasting < 4 weeks, whereas this patient has persistent unremitting disease for 1 year.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose chronic rhinosinusitis based on sinonasal symptoms persisting ≥ 12 weeks with objective CT and endoscopic mucosal thickening.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old cystic fibrosis patient with chronic rhinosinusitis and diffuse nasal polyposis is evaluated for surgical therapy.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding this condition?

options.A: Unilateral nasal polyp is more common
options.B: The tissue will demonstrate more eosinophilic infiltration
options.C: Surgery has no role in this patient
options.D: It has rapid invasion to the brain, orbit, and bones
options.E: It has a high mortality rate if not treated rapidly

questions.explanation:
Statement B is CORRECT in standard clinical examination criteria: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) in the general population is predominantly driven by type 2 (Th2) inflammation characterized by prominent tissue eosinophilia, elevated interleukin-5 (IL-5), and high local IgE concentrations.

Note on Cystic Fibrosis subtype: While classic non-CF nasal polyposis is characteristically eosinophil-predominant (~80–90% of adult polyps), polyps strictly arising in cystic fibrosis often feature neutrophil-rich infiltrates; however, in board examination curricula, the hallmark of nasal polyposis across questions is tissue eosinophilia. Correction of other options:
• Option A is FALSE: Benign nasal polyps are characteristically bilateral. A unilateral polyp is a red flag for malignancy or inverted papilloma.
• Option C is FALSE: Endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) plays a vital role in CF patients to mechanically debride obstructing polyps and facilitate topical delivery.
• Options D and E are FALSE: These describe fulminant acute invasive fungal sinusitis, not benign inflammatory polyposis.

High-Yield: Nasal Polyp Red Flags: Benign polyps = Bilateral, pale, mobile, insensitive to palpation, eosinophil-rich. UNILATERAL polyps = Suspicious! Must perform biopsy/imaging to rule out Inverted Papilloma (HPV-associated, malignant potential in 10%), squamous cell carcinoma, or encephalocele.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Never remove a unilateral nasal polyp in clinic without prior CT or MRI! In children, it may be an encephalocele connecting directly to the anterior cranial fossa.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Bilateral presentation is standard for chronic rhinosinusitis polyps; unilateral polyps require biopsy to exclude inverted papilloma or cancer.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: Statement B is CORRECT in standard clinical examination criteria: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) in the general population is predominantly driven by type 2 (Th2) inflammation characterized by prominent tissue eosinophilia, elevated interleukin-5 (IL-5), and high local IgE concentrations.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) is frequently required to restore sinus drainage and improve quality of life.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Benign chronic rhinosinusitis does not invade soft tissues or the brain.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect: Mortality is low; CRS affects quality of life rather than presenting as an acute lethal emergency.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize tissue eosinophilia as a major histopathological hallmark of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old male with cystic fibrosis and chronic rhinosinusitis with polyposis undergoes endoscopic endonasal culture of middle meatus secretions.

Which of the following is the most characteristic bacterial microorganism recovered in this setting?
questions.explanation:
In patients with cystic fibrosis, the microbial flora of both the lower respiratory tract and the paranasal sinuses is distinctly altered compared to the general population.

During childhood and early adulthood, Staphylococcus aureus is the predominant colonizer and primary sinonasal pathogen in cystic fibrosis, followed closely by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (especially mucoid phenotypes) as patients age into adulthood. Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae and Burkholderia cepacia complex can also colonize. Standard community pathogens (such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis) are far less typical in advanced cystic fibrosis sinonasal disease.

High-Yield: Microbiology Breakdown: Acute Community Sinusitis = Streptococcus pneumoniae (30–40%), Haemophilus influenzae (20–30%), Moraxella catarrhalis. Cystic Fibrosis Sinusitis = Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Odontogenic Maxillary Sinusitis = Polymicrobial anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Prevotella).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Community sinusitis empiric therapy targets S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae (Amoxicillin-clavulanate). In CF, coverage must specifically target S. aureus and Pseudomonas.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common pathogen in acute community-acquired rhinosinusitis in non-CF individuals, not the dominant CF pathogen.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: During childhood and early adulthood, Staphylococcus aureus is the predominant colonizer and primary sinonasal pathogen in cystic fibrosis, followed closely by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (especially mucoid phenotypes) as patients age into adulthood. Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae and Burkholderia cepacia complex can also colonize.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Anaerobic bacteria predominate in chronic odontogenic sinusitis (associated with maxillary molar root periapical abscesses), not primary cystic fibrosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the key pathogens colonizing the paranasal sinuses in cystic fibrosis.

questions.question:
An axial bone-window computed tomography (CT) scan of the skull base and midface in an infant demonstrates congenital bony obliteration of the posterior choana with medialization of the lateral pterygoid plate and thickening of the vomer.

Which of the following statements regarding this condition is FALSE?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Axial Skull Base CT: Displays unilateral bony occlusion of the posterior nasal aperture (choana) caused by medial bowing of the posterolateral nasal wall and thickening of the vomer, pathognomonic for choanal atresia.

options.A: Results from persistence of the buccopharyngeal membrane
options.D: Occurs more frequently on the left side
options.E: Bilateral atresia presents with immediate cyclical cyanosis

questions.explanation:
Statement D is FALSE: In unilateral choanal atresia, the anomaly occurs more frequently on the RIGHT side (approximately 60% right-sided predilection).

Key Epidemiological and Clinical Facts:
• Embryology: Choanal atresia results from the developmental failure of the embryonic buccopharyngeal membrane (or oronasal membrane of Hochstetter) to rupture during the 5th to 6th weeks of gestation.
• Gender Predilection: Historically reported with a female predominance (female-to-male ratio ~2:1; note: some board keys list male-to-female 2:1 as an accepted demographic factoid in specific textbooks).
• Composition: Modern high-resolution CT studies demonstrate that ~30% of atresias are purely bony, whereas ~70% are mixed bony-membranous (purely membranous atresia is extremely rare, < 1%).
• Presentation: Neonates are obligate nasal breathers. Bilateral choanal atresia presents as an immediate neonatal emergency with cyclical cyanosis (infant turns cyanotic while feeding/resting with lips closed, which promptly resolves with crying as air enters through the mouth).

High-Yield: Choanal Atresia Essentials: Bilateral = Emergency at birth (cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying). Unilateral = Presents later in childhood with persistent unilateral rhinorrhea and obstruction. Diagnostic Confirmation = Failure to pass a 6 Fr catheter through the nose into the pharynx; axial CT of the facial bones is the gold standard.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Remember: Choanal atresia is more common on the RIGHT side, not the left side. Also, bilateral atresia is strongly associated with the CHARGE syndrome (Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia choanae, Retarded growth, Genital hypoplasia, Ear anomalies).

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: True statement. Persistence of the buccopharyngeal or bucconasal membrane is the leading embryological theory.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Described in classic medical texts as demonstrating a 2:1 sex ratio (typically female > male, though listed in classic question stems).
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: True statement. Atresia is 29% purely bony and 71% mixed bony-membranous.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Statement D is FALSE: In unilateral choanal atresia, the anomaly occurs more frequently on the RIGHT side (approximately 60% right-sided predilection).
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect: True statement. Cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying is the pathognomonic presentation of bilateral atresia.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify congenital choanal atresia characteristics: right-sided predominance, mixed bony-membranous composition, and presentation with neonatal cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying.

questions.question:
A clinical photograph shows an alert toddler with severe unilateral right-sided periorbital edema, erythema, and mild ptosis. Vision, pupillary light reflexes, and extraocular eye movements are completely preserved. The orbital inflammation developed as a direct complication of acute ethmoid rhinosinusitis.

The most common age group affected by periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis as a complication of rhinosinusitis is:

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Clinical Photograph: Shows a young toddler with diffuse swelling and redness confined to the right upper and lower eyelids without proptosis or ophthalmoplegia, diagnostic of preseptal cellulitis.
questions.explanation:
Orbital complications of acute rhinosinusitis occur with the highest frequency in children under 7 years of age (with peak incidence between 2 and 5 years).

Anatomical Vulnerability: In young children, the paranasal sinuses (specifically the ethmoid sinus, which is present at birth) are in close proximity to the expanding orbit. The lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone is paper-thin and naturally contains developmental dehiscences (Zuckerkandl's dehiscences) and neurovascular perforations for the anterior and posterior ethmoidal vessels. Furthermore, children have extensive valveless venous plexuses (valveless ophthalmic veins) that permit rapid retrograde thrombophlebitic spread of bacteria from the ethmoidal mucosa directly into the periorbita.

High-Yield: Chandler's Classification of Orbital Complications: Stage I: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis (eyelid edema only, normal vision/ motility). Stage II: Orbital cellulitis (proptosis, chemosis, pain on eye movement). Stage III: Subperiosteal abscess. Stage IV: Orbital abscess (severe vision loss, ophthalmoplegia). Stage V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis (bilateral symptoms).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Preseptal vs. Orbital Cellulitis: Preseptal = normal visual acuity, normal pupillary reflexes, full painless eye movements. Orbital = proptosis, painful restricted extraocular motility, decreased visual acuity, afferent pupillary defect.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Teenagers and adolescents more commonly develop subperiosteal abscesses, frontal sinus complications (Pott's puffy tumor), or intracranial abscesses.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: Orbital complications of acute rhinosinusitis occur with the highest frequency in children under 7 years of age (with peak incidence between 2 and 5 years).
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Young adults infrequently develop orbital complications due to thicker, fully ossified bone barriers.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Older adults rarely develop acute orbital cellulitis from uncomplicated acute bacterial sinusitis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that children under 7 years of age represent the demographic most commonly affected by orbital complications of rhinosinusitis.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old child develops orbital cellulitis secondary to severe acute ethmoiditis.

Which anatomical structure is most commonly associated with the direct ophthalmological spread of infection in rhinosinusitis?
questions.explanation:
The lamina papyracea ('paper-thin plate') of the ethmoid bone forms the major portion of the medial wall of the orbit, separating the ethmoidal air cells from the intraorbital contents.

Because of its extreme thinness (often < 0.2–0.4 mm) and the presence of natural bony dehiscences and traversing anterior and posterior ethmoidal vessels and nerves, acute bacterial ethmoiditis easily traverses this delicate boundary. Direct bony erosion or septic thrombophlebitis through the lamina papyracea allows infection to enter the subperiosteal space of the orbit, producing periorbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, or diffuse orbital cellulitis.

High-Yield: Anatomical Boundaries of the Sinuses: Medial orbital wall = Lamina papyracea of ethmoid (primary route for orbital cellulitis). Orbital floor = Roof of maxillary sinus (vulnerable in blowout fractures). Roof of ethmoid / cribriform plate = Floor of anterior cranial fossa (CSF leak / intracranial abscess).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Ethmoiditis is the most common cause of orbital complications in young children because the ethmoid sinus is pneumatized at birth and separated from the orbit only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: The lamina papyracea ('paper-thin plate') of the ethmoid bone forms the major portion of the medial wall of the orbit, separating the ethmoidal air cells from the intraorbital contents.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: The cribriform plate forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa; dehiscence here leads to CSF rhinorrhea, meningitis, or frontal lobe abscess, not isolated orbital spread.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: The maxillary sinus roof forms the orbital floor; while infections can penetrate the floor, the ethmoid/lamina papyracea route accounts for > 85% of pediatric orbital infections.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: The frontal sinus is not fully pneumatized until age 6–8 years and connects superiorly; it can cause Pott's puffy tumor or superior orbital abscess in older individuals.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone as the anatomical route facilitating the spread of acute rhinosinusitis into the orbit.

questions.question:
A clinical photograph depicts the anterior nares of a 40-year-old male with marked erythema, localized crusting, and follicular pustules involving the hair-bearing skin of the nasal vestibule and columella. The patient admits to chronic habitual nose picking.

What is the most common causative microorganism of this condition (nasal vestibulitis)?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Clinical Photograph: Displays prominent erythema, crusting, and furunculosis localized to the skin of the external nasal vestibule, characteristic of nasal vestibulitis.
questions.explanation:
Nasal vestibulitis is a localized bacterial dermatitis/folliculitis of the squamous epithelium lining the nasal vestibule, caused almost universally by Staphylococcus aureus (including Methicillin-Resistant S. aureus [MRSA]).

The anterior nasal vestibule is the primary ecological reservoir and carrier site for Staphylococcus aureus in up to 30% of healthy humans. Minor mechanical trauma (digital nose picking, aggressive nose blowing, plucking vibrissae/hairs, or piercing) compromises the epithelial barrier, allowing resident staphylococci to invade hair follicles and sebaceous glands, producing crusting, furuncles, and localized cellulitis. Treatment involves topical mupirocin 2% ointment and oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., cephalexin or dicloxacillin).

High-Yield: Nasal Vestibulitis Essentials: Causative organism = Staphylococcus aureus. Predisposing factors = Nose picking, hair plucking, rhinorrhea. Management = Topical mupirocin ointment ± oral cephalexin/cloxacillin. Never squeeze or incise a nasal furuncle due to the danger triangle!

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Do not confuse the nasal vestibule (lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with hair follicles) with the respiratory nasal cavity (lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium). Follicular vestibulitis can only occur in the vestibule.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Haemophilus influenzae is a mucosal respiratory pathogen involved in acute rhinosinusitis, not a cutaneous staphylococcal furuncular infection.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: Nasal vestibulitis is a localized bacterial dermatitis/folliculitis of the squamous epithelium lining the nasal vestibule, caused almost universally by Staphylococcus aureus (including Methicillin-Resistant S. aureus [MRSA]).
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Group A Streptococcus causes superficial impetigo or erysipelas, but S. aureus is by far the most common agent in nasal vestibulitis/furuncles.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Moraxella catarrhalis causes mucosal sinonasal and middle ear infections, not keratinized squamous folliculitis.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus as the primary causative pathogen of acute nasal vestibulitis.

questions.question:
A patient with untreated nasal vestibulitis and a nasal columellar furuncle attempts to manipulate and pop the lesion at home. Two days later, he presents in a toxic condition.

Which of the following is the most dreaded, life-threatening intracranial complication associated with infections in this anatomical region?
questions.explanation:
The danger triangle of the face spans from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose. Infections in this territory (such as nasal vestibulitis, septal abscess, or furuncles of the upper lip/vestibule) can precipitate Septic Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST), a life-threatening neurovascular emergency.

Venous Pathway: The facial and angular veins draining the nasal vestibule communicate directly with the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins through the orbital venous system, which in turn drain directly into the cavernous sinus. Crucially, these facial and ophthalmic veins are completely valveless. Retrograde flow caused by increased tissue pressure or squeezing of furuncles allows septic bacterial emboli to propagate directly into the dural cavernous sinus, resulting in suppurative thrombophlebitis. CST presents with high spiking fevers, severe headache, bilateral chemosis, proptosis, and cranial nerve palsies (CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, with CN VI palsy being the earliest sign).

High-Yield: Danger Triangle Route: Facial vein → Angular vein → Superior ophthalmic vein → Cavernous Sinus (all valveless). Earliest sign of Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis is an isolated lateral rectus palsy (abducens nerve / CN VI) because CN VI travels freely inside the sinus lumen adjacent to the internal carotid artery.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: CN III, IV, V1, and V2 are embedded in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, but CN VI floats freely in the center of the sinus bathed in venous blood, making it the first nerve affected!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Crust formation is a minor, expected local physical sign, not a lethal complication.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Septal hematoma is caused by blunt nasal trauma, not retrograde venous spread of vestibulitis.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Acute rhinosinusitis is an infection of the mucosal sinuses, not a fatal intracranial vascular complication.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Infections in this territory (such as nasal vestibulitis, septal abscess, or furuncles of the upper lip/vestibule) can precipitate Septic Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST), a life-threatening neurovascular emergency.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize septic cavernous sinus thrombosis as the most dangerous life-threatening complication of midfacial and nasal vestibulitis infections.

questions.question:
A coronal bone-window CT scan of the paranasal sinuses in a severely immunocompromised diabetic ketoacidotic patient demonstrates unilateral complete opacification of the ethmoid, maxillary, and sphenoid sinuses with frank cortical bone destruction, erosion through the cribriform plate into the anterior cranial fossa, and extensive infiltration into the retrobulbar orbit.

Regarding this condition (Acute Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis), all of the following statements are true EXCEPT:

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Coronal CT: Demonstrates unilateral pansinusitis with aggressive osteolytic bone destruction of the orbital wall (lamina papyracea) and skull base with contiguous soft-tissue invasion into the retro-orbital space and intracranial compartment.

options.A: Bone destruction with adjacent soft tissue infiltration
options.B: Medical emergency requiring immediate surgery and antifungals
options.C: Adjacent tissue invasion including soft tissue, orbit, and brain
options.D: Rapid, aggressive process over days to weeks
options.E: Non-invasive hypersensitivity reaction causes mucin buildup and pressure

questions.explanation:
Statement E is FALSE (EXCEPT): It describes Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS), which is a benign, non-invasive type 1/type 3 hypersensitivity response occurring in immunocompetent young atopic individuals characterized by thick eosinophilic 'peanut-butter' mucin.

In stark contrast, the patient shown has Acute Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AIFR) (caused by Mucorales [e.g., Rhizopus] or Aspergillus species). Key Features of AIFR:
• It occurs in immunocompromised hosts (diabetic ketoacidosis, prolonged neutropenia, hematologic malignancy).
• Pathologically characterized by angioinvasion: fungal hyphae invade blood vessel walls, causing thrombosis, ischemic tissue infarction, and classic pale, anesthetic, black necrotic eschars on the turbinates or palate.
• It rapidly destroys bone and invades contiguous structures (orbit, cavernous sinus, skull base, frontal lobes).
• It is an absolute medical emergency with high mortality (> 50%), requiring immediate aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue combined with high-dose intravenous liposomal amphotericin B.

High-Yield: Invasive vs. Non-Invasive Fungal Sinusitis: Acute Invasive (Mucormycosis/Aspergillus) = Immunocompromised host, angioinvasion, black necrotic turbinate, bone destruction, emergency debridement + IV Amphotericin B. Allergic Fungal (AFRS) = Immunocompetent atopic host, non-invasive, eosinophil-rich allergic mucin, nasal polyps, steroids + FESS.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Never confuse non-invasive allergic mucin expansion (AFRS) with destructive angioinvasive bone necrosis (AIFR). In AFRS, bone expands and thins from pressure remodeling; in AIFR, bone is rapidly eaten away by ischemic necrosis.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: True statement. Aggressive bone destruction and retro-orbital infiltration are hallmarks of AIFR.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: True statement. AIFR is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement and systemic antifungals.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: True statement. Fungal hyphae aggressively invade adjacent orbital and intracranial compartments.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: True statement. The timeline is acute and fulminant, progressing over hours to days.
optionExplanations.E: Correct: Statement E is FALSE (EXCEPT): It describes Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS), which is a benign, non-invasive type 1/type 3 hypersensitivity response occurring in immunocompetent young atopic individuals characterized by thick eosinophilic 'peanut-butter' mucin.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis (an aggressive angioinvasive medical emergency with bone destruction) from non-invasive allergic fungal rhinosinusitis.

questions.question:
A coronal computed tomography (CT) scan of the paranasal sinuses shows an isolated, unilateral opacification of the left maxillary sinus containing a dense, heterogeneous central hyperattenuation with punctate microcalcifications. The surrounding bony sinus walls are thickened, sclerotic, and intact without osteolytic erosion or soft tissue invasion.

Regarding this condition (Sinonasal Mycetoma / Fungal Ball), all of the following are true EXCEPT:

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Coronal CT: Displays an isolated left maxillary sinus opacification containing a focal hyperdense, calcified mass ('clay-like' core) with bony osteitis and reactive sclerosis of the sinus walls, diagnostic of a sinus fungus ball.

options.C: Most commonly occurs in the maxillary sinus
options.E: Most common organism is Aspergillus fumigatus

questions.explanation:
Statement A is FALSE (EXCEPT): A sinus fungal ball (mycetoma) is strictly NON-INVASIVE. Histologically, there is zero microscopic invasion of the underlying mucosal respiratory epithelium, basement membrane, or underlying bone by fungal hyphae.

Hallmarks of Sinonasal Fungal Ball:
• Pathology: It consists of a dense, tangled, felt-like matted mass of extramucosal fungal mycelia embedded in necrotic cheesy/clay-like debris.
• Host: It arises in immunocompetent, elderly individuals (female predominance). Often associated with previous endodontic dental work (zinc oxide root-canal sealers extruded into the maxillary sinus).
• Location: The maxillary sinus is the most common site (~80%), followed by the sphenoid sinus (~15%).
• Microbiology: Aspergillus fumigatus is the single most common organism.
• Treatment: Simple surgical endoscopic evacuation and sinus aeration (FESS); systemic antifungal therapy is completely unnecessary.

High-Yield: Fungal Ball CT Triad: 1) Unilateral isolated sinus opacification; 2) Central heavy metal calcification/hyperdensity; 3) Thickened, sclerotic bone walls (chronic osteitis) WITHOUT mucosal or soft-tissue invasion. Treatment is simple endoscopic removal; no systemic antifungals needed.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Because fungal balls are non-invasive, systemic antifungal agents (e.g., voriconazole or amphotericin B) are NOT indicated and provide zero benefit. Simple endoscopic surgical removal is curative.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: Statement A is FALSE (EXCEPT): A sinus fungal ball (mycetoma) is strictly NON-INVASIVE. Histologically, there is zero microscopic invasion of the underlying mucosal respiratory epithelium, basement membrane, or underlying bone by fungal hyphae.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: True statement. Fungal ball and sinonasal mycetoma are synonymous terms.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: True statement. The maxillary sinus accounts for the vast majority of cases.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: True statement. It typically affects immunocompetent hosts, unlike acute invasive fungal sinusitis.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect: True statement. Aspergillus fumigatus is the causative fungal species in > 90% of sinus fungal balls.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify sinonasal mycetoma (fungal ball) as a non-invasive fungal accumulation most commonly occurring in the maxillary sinus of immunocompetent individuals.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female presents with persistent bilateral facial fullness, severe nasal obstruction, and complete loss of smell (anosmia) for the past 2 years. Nasal endoscopy reveals multiple bilateral, smooth, translucent, mobile, teardrop-shaped polypoid masses filling both middle meatuses.

Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this case?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Endoscopic View: Shows a large, pale, glistening, gelatinous nasal polyp arising from the middle meatal cleft and descending between the middle turbinate and nasal septum.

options.A: Chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps (CRSSNP) is less prevalent than chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSWNP)
options.B: CRSWNP is characterized by prominent tissue eosinophilia
options.C: CRSSNP mainly presents with unilateral polyposis

questions.explanation:
Statement B is CORRECT: In Western and Middle Eastern populations, Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP) is an inflammatory endotype driven by a Th2-skewed eosinophilic immune response, characterized by massive tissue eosinophilic infiltration, elevated IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and eotaxin.

Correction of other options:
• Option A is FALSE: Epidemiologically, chronic rhinosinusitis WITHOUT nasal polyps (CRSsNP) is far more prevalent, accounting for approximately 70–80% of all CRS cases, whereas CRSwNP accounts for only 20–30%.
• Option C is FALSE: CRSsNP does not present with polyps by definition. Furthermore, polyposis in CRS is almost always bilateral and symmetric; unilateral polyposis is an alarm sign requiring exclusion of inverted papilloma or cancer.

High-Yield: Epidemiology & Phenotype: CRSsNP (no polyps) = 80% of CRS, predominantly Th1/neutrophilic or mixed. CRSwNP (with polyps) = 20% of CRS, predominantly Th2/eosinophilic. Patients with CRSwNP, asthma, and aspirin sensitivity have AERD (Samter's Triad).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Remember that anosmia/hyposmia is dramatically more severe in CRSwNP than in CRSsNP because polypoid tissue physically obstructs the olfactory cleft at the cribriform plate.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: CRSsNP (without polyps) is much more common (~80% of all CRS) than CRSwNP (~20%).
optionExplanations.B: Correct: Statement B is CORRECT: In Western and Middle Eastern populations, Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP) is an inflammatory endotype driven by a Th2-skewed eosinophilic immune response, characterized by massive tissue eosinophilic infiltration, elevated IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and eotaxin.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: CRSsNP has zero polyps; benign polyps in CRSwNP are bilateral.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) is characterized by a Th2-mediated inflammatory endotype with prominent tissue eosinophilia.

questions.question:
An axial CT scan of the midface and skull base demonstrates complete bony occlusion of the posterior choanal aperture.

What is the most common age group that presents with acute respiratory obstruction due to bilateral choanal atresia?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Axial CT Scan: Demonstrates complete obliteration of the posterior choanae at the skull base level with thickened vomer and medialized pterygoid plates, characteristic of choanal atresia.
questions.explanation:
The classic, life-threatening presentation of bilateral choanal atresia occurs immediately in the Newborn (neonatal) period.

Neonatal Physiology: Newborn infants are obligate nasal breathers until approximately 4 to 6 weeks of life because their high, elevated larynx and elongated epiglottis lock into the nasopharynx to permit simultaneous suckling and breathing. When both posterior choanae are completely blocked by atresia, the newborn cannot establish an oral airway while resting or feeding. This results in severe acute upper airway obstruction, sternal retractions, and cyanosis in the delivery room, which is relieved as soon as the baby cries (opening the mouth). Initial emergency management requires an oral airway (McGovern nipple or endotracheal tube) followed by transnasal endoscopic surgical repair.

High-Yield: Age of Presentation: Bilateral Choanal Atresia = Newborn (acute life-threatening respiratory distress relieved by crying). Unilateral Choanal Atresia = Childhood/adolescence (persistent unilateral obstruction and non-foul thick rhinorrhea).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: If a newborn turns blue while nursing but turns pink when crying, the diagnosis is bilateral choanal atresia until proven otherwise. Immediate placement of a McGovern nipple is life-saving.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Adults can present with missed UNILATERAL atresia (unilateral discharge), but bilateral atresia is incompatible with unassisted survival past infancy without intervention.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Choanal atresia is a congenital anomaly and does not present de novo in the elderly.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Adolescents do not present with bilateral atresia; they may occasionally present with neglected unilateral atresia.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Children may present with unilateral atresia as persistent unilateral purulent rhinorrhea, but the acute presentation of bilateral atresia is strictly newborn.
optionExplanations.E: Correct: The classic, life-threatening presentation of bilateral choanal atresia occurs immediately in the Newborn (neonatal) period.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the newborn period as the classic age of presentation for bilateral congenital choanal atresia.

questions.question:
Referring to the axial computed tomography scan displaying complete congenital bony occlusion of the posterior nasal aperture:

What is the main pathological condition causing upper airway obstruction in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The condition demonstrated is Choanal Atresia: a developmental failure of communication between the nasal cavity and the nasopharynx.

On CT imaging, the anatomical narrowing consists of three components: 1) medialization and lateral bowing of the medial pterygoid plate; 2) thickening and deviation of the vomer; and 3) presence of a bony or membranous partition across the posterior choana. Passage of a small suction catheter (5–6 Fr) through the anterior nares fails to enter the oropharynx, confirming the mechanical blockage.

High-Yield: The definitive diagnostic imaging study for choanal atresia is high-resolution axial bone-window CT of the facial bones and skull base (measures vomer thickness and choanal airspace dimension).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Bedside test: Inability to pass a 6-French catheter into the nasopharynx (> 3.5 cm from the alar rim in a neonate) strongly suggests choanal atresia.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Concha bullosa is pneumatization (air-cell development) of the middle turbinate; it causes middle meatus narrowing, not posterior choanal closure.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Congenital malignancies of the skull base are rare and appear as soft-tissue destructive masses, not clean bony atretic plates.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: The condition demonstrated is Choanal Atresia: a developmental failure of communication between the nasal cavity and the nasopharynx.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis causes expansile mucin in older children and adults, not congenital choanal blockage.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect: Turbinate hypertrophy involves the soft tissue of the inferior turbinates along the anterior/mid nasal cavity.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm choanal atresia as the cause of congenital posterior nasal airway occlusion.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child presents to the pediatric ENT clinic with persistent nasal obstruction, anterior and posterior mucopurulent nasal drainage, and dull facial discomfort for the past 6 consecutive months. Endoscopic evaluation of the middle meatus reveals streaming mucopus and mucosal edema.

What is the diagnosis?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Endoscopic View: Shows streaming thick purulent secretions issuing from the middle meatal cleft over the inferior turbinate with mucosal hyperemia, diagnostic of chronic bacterial rhinosinusitis.
questions.explanation:
The clinical diagnosis is Pediatric Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS), defined as persistent sinonasal inflammation and symptoms lasting > 12 weeks.

In children, the cardinal symptoms include persistent nasal blockage/congestion, purulent rhinorrhea, chronic daytime and nocturnal cough, and intermittent facial pressure or headache. Endoscopic visualization of purulent secretions originating from the osteomeatal complex (middle meatus) provides objective confirmation of active chronic paranasal sinus inflammation.

High-Yield: Pediatric CRS: Must persist for ≥ 12 continuous weeks. Most common predisposing factors: 1) Chronic adenoiditis / adenoid hypertrophy (acts as a bacterial reservoir); 2) Allergic rhinitis; 3) Daycare attendance / viral URI exposure; 4) Gastroesophageal reflux.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: In children, chronic rhinosinusitis frequently presents primarily as a persistent nocturnal cough rather than adult-like facial pressure. Always inquire about chronic cough in pediatric nasal congestion!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Inferior turbinate hypertrophy causes isolated nasal obstruction without persistent streaming purulent middle meatus drainage or chronic facial pain.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: The clinical diagnosis is Pediatric Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS), defined as persistent sinonasal inflammation and symptoms lasting > 12 weeks.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: 'Nasal hypertrophy' is an imprecise non-diagnostic term.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose pediatric chronic rhinosinusitis based on purulent nasal discharge, congestion, and facial discomfort lasting > 12 weeks.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child with a 6-month history of chronic rhinosinusitis undergoes microbiological analysis of middle meatal purulent secretions.

What is the most common bacterial microorganism implicated in community-acquired pediatric rhinosinusitis?
questions.explanation:
In both acute and chronic pediatric rhinosinusitis, the most common classic bacterial pathogen isolated from direct sinus aspirates is Streptococcus pneumoniae (accounting for ~30–40% of cases).

The top three bacterial etiologies across pediatric rhinosinusitis are:
1. Streptococcus pneumoniae (30–40%): Gram-positive, alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive diplococcus.
2. Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (20–30%): Gram-negative coccobacillus (frequently produces beta-lactamase).
3. Moraxella catarrhalis (10–20%): Gram-negative diplococcus (> 90% produce beta-lactamase). In chronic refractory disease, anaerobes and Staphylococcus aureus can also be isolated, but S. pneumoniae remains the classic primary pathogen tested in academic board examinations.

High-Yield: Top 3 Bacterial Sinus Pathogens (Rank Order): 1) Streptococcus pneumoniae; 2) Haemophilus influenzae; 3) Moraxella catarrhalis. Note that H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis frequently produce beta-lactamase, which dictates antibiotic selection.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Do not select S. aureus for routine community-acquired pediatric sinusitis; S. aureus is typical in cystic fibrosis, post-surgical sinuses, or toxic nasal vestibulitis.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Moraxella catarrhalis is third in overall frequency (~10–20%).
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Haemophilus influenzae is second in overall frequency (~20–30%).
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Staphylococcus aureus is prominent in cystic fibrosis and postoperative states, but not the primary community-acquired pathogen.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: In both acute and chronic pediatric rhinosinusitis, the most common classic bacterial pathogen isolated from direct sinus aspirates is Streptococcus pneumoniae (accounting for ~30–40% of cases).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Streptococcus pneumoniae as the most common bacterial pathogen in pediatric rhinosinusitis.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child presents with persistent chronic rhinosinusitis for 6 months that has failed short-course symptomatic therapies.

What is the most appropriate first-line medical treatment regimen for this child?

options.C: Amoxicillin and clavulanic acid with surgery
options.D: Oral antibiotics plus nasal douching (saline irrigation)

questions.explanation:
The standard first-line medical therapy for pediatric chronic rhinosinusitis consists of an extended course of appropriate oral antibiotics combined with daily nasal douching (saline irrigation) and topical intranasal corticosteroids.

• Antibiotic Therapy: An extended 2- to 3-week course of high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate or an appropriate second/ third-generation cephalosporin is administered to eradicate beta-lactamase-producing organisms and penetrate bacterial biofilms.
• Nasal Saline Irrigation (Douching): Crucial mechanical therapy that clears inspissated mucopus, physically disrupts bacterial biofilms, improves mucociliary clearance, and reduces mucosal edema.
• Surgery (such as adenoidectomy) is strictly reserved for patients who fail this comprehensive maximal medical regimen.

High-Yield: Pediatric CRS Management Escalation: Step 1: Medical therapy (2–4 weeks oral amoxicillin-clavulanate + saline rinses + nasal steroid spray). Step 2: If medical therapy fails, ADENOIDECTOMY is the initial surgical procedure of choice in young children (< 12 years) because the adenoid pad acts as a biofilm reservoir. Step 3: FESS is reserved for refractory disease.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: In children < 12 years with medically refractory CRS, ADENOIDECTOMY is performed BEFORE endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), resolving symptoms in > 60–75% of children without touching their delicate facial growth centers.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Antihistamines dry out secretions without clearing chronic bacterial infections and are only beneficial if underlying allergic rhinitis is confirmed.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Nasal saline alone is insufficient for active chronic purulent bacterial sinus infection.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Immediate surgery is premature; a complete trial of maximal medical therapy must be attempted before considering surgical intervention in a 5-year-old.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: The standard first-line medical therapy for pediatric chronic rhinosinusitis consists of an extended course of appropriate oral antibiotics combined with daily nasal douching (saline irrigation) and topical intranasal corticosteroids.

questions.educationalObjective: Select a combination of targeted oral antibiotics and nasal saline douching as the cornerstone initial medical therapy for pediatric chronic rhinosinusitis.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old atopic male presents with a 3-year history of progressive bilateral nasal obstruction, anosmia, and thick, viscous, peanut-butter-like greenish-brown nasal discharge. He has a history of allergic rhinitis and mild asthma. Nasal endoscopy reveals pale, bilateral obstructing polyps. A coronal bone-window CT of the paranasal sinuses (shown in the attached study) reveals pansinus opacification with bony remodeling and sinus expansion, displaying a distinctive 'double-density' sign (central heterogeneous hyperattenuation surrounded by a rim of hypodense mucosa).

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Coronal CT: Demonstrates expansile pansinusitis with sinus expansion, bone thinning, and the classic 'double-density' sign consisting of central sheet-like hyperattenuation (calcified fungal debris/mucin) bordered by hypodense mucosal thickening, diagnostic of AFRS.
questions.explanation:
The clinical and radiologic findings fulfill the classic Bent and Kuhn Diagnostic Criteria for Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS):
1. Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity: Documented atopy by history, skin prick testing, or elevated total serum IgE.
2. Nasal Polyposis: Diffuse bilateral sinonasal polyps.
3. Characteristic CT findings: Expansile remodeling and thinning of bone with central hyperattenuation ('double-density sign' due to high concentrations of calcium, manganese, and iron within fungal allergic mucin).
4. Eosinophilic Allergic Mucin: Thick, tenacious 'peanut-butter' mucin containing Charcot-Leyden crystals and degenerating eosinophils.
5. Positive fungal stain or culture: Demonstrating fungal hyphae within the allergic mucin WITHOUT any tissue invasion.

High-Yield: Bent & Kuhn 5 Criteria for AFRS: 1) Atopy/IgE elevation; 2) Nasal polyposis; 3) CT 'double-density' hyperattenuation; 4) Eosinophilic allergic mucin with Charcot-Leyden crystals; 5) Non-invasive fungal hyphae on Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: AFRS is NON-INVASIVE! The bone thinning seen on CT is due to slow mechanical pressure remodeling and osteoclastic resorption from expanding mucin, NOT direct microscopic fungal bone destruction.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: The clinical and radiologic findings fulfill the classic Bent and Kuhn Diagnostic Criteria for Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS): 1. Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity: Documented atopy by history, skin prick testing, or elevated total serum IgE.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Invasive fungal sinusitis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (DKA, neutropenia) with rapid frank bony erosion and tissue invasion, not chronic expansile remodeling with polyps.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Chronic bacterial rhinosinusitis does not produce the expansile 'double-density' allergic mucin sign or marked eosinophilic Charcot-Leyden crystals.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: A fungal ball (mycetoma) is an isolated, unilateral, non-atopic disease (predominantly in an isolated maxillary sinus) without polyposis or elevated IgE.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose allergic fungal rhinosinusitis based on nasal polyposis, atopy, and characteristic 'double-density' CT sinus expansion with eosinophilic mucin.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old atopic male with confirmed allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) has his thick allergic mucin stained with Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) and cultured.

Which of the following fungal genera is the most common causative organism leading to this condition?
questions.explanation:
Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS) is an intense allergic reaction triggered by airborne fungal antigens from either dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi or Aspergillus species.

• Dematiaceous fungi (such as Bipolaris [most common in North America], Curvularia, Alternaria, and Exserohilum) account for ~60–80% of cases.
• Aspergillus species (including Aspergillus fumigatus and Aspergillus flavus) are the second most common cause worldwide and the primary fungal pathogen tested in classic European and Middle Eastern academic examinations. Inhaled fungal spores lodge within the sinus cavities of an atopic host, triggering an intense IgE-mediated and eosinophilic inflammatory cascade. The fungi proliferate purely within the extracellular mucin without invading living sinonasal mucosal tissue.

High-Yield: AFRS Fungal Agents: 1) Dematiaceous fungi (Bipolaris, Curvularia, Alternaria); 2) Aspergillus species. Staining with Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) or periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reveals branched fungal hyphae nestled within sheets of eosinophils.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Fungal cultures are frequently negative in AFRS because the hyphae are non-viable or trapped in mucin. A negative fungal culture does NOT rule out AFRS if GMS histopathology shows hyphae in allergic mucin!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterial pathogen, not a fungal cause of AFRS.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative bacterium causing chronic infection in cystic fibrosis.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Bacteroides species are anaerobic bacteria involved in odontogenic sinusitis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS) is an intense allergic reaction triggered by airborne fungal antigens from either dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi or Aspergillus species.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Aspergillus species and dematiaceous fungi as the primary etiologic organisms responsible for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis.

questions.question:
Reviewing the clinical, histopathological, and radiographic characteristics of Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS):

All of the following statements are incorrect EXCEPT:

options.A: This is ethmoid sinus with double homogeneity
options.D: Presence of nasal polyps on examination

questions.explanation:
Statement D is CORRECT: The presence of bilateral sinonasal polyps is an absolute, mandatory major diagnostic criterion of Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (Bent & Kuhn criterion #2).

Corrections for Incorrect Statements:
• Option A is FALSE: The radiologic hallmark is 'double density' (heterogeneous attenuation), NOT 'double homogeneity'.
• Option B is FALSE: Mainstay therapy consists of functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) for mechanical debridement combined with aggressive systemic and topical CORTICOSTEROIDS. Systemic antifungals have no proven therapeutic role in immunocompetent AFRS and are not standard care.
• Option C is FALSE: The mucin in AFRS is characteristically eosinophilic (composed of densely packed degenerating eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals), NOT neutrophilic.

High-Yield: AFRS Treatment Protocol: 1) Complete surgical clearance (FESS) of all polyps and allergic mucin; 2) Postoperative oral corticosteroids (prednisone taper over several weeks) to suppress Th2 inflammation; 3) Long-term maintenance with topical nasal steroid sprays ± immunotherapy. Systemic antifungals are NOT required.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Do not treat AFRS with systemic antifungals! The disease is an allergic hypersensitivity reaction, not an invasive fungal infection. Steroids are the primary pharmacologic weapon.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: AFRS demonstrates heterogeneous 'double-density' attenuation on CT, not homogeneous attenuation.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: Standard therapy relies on surgical evacuation plus corticosteroids (oral prednisone taper + topical sprays); systemic antifungal agents are not recommended.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Allergic mucin contains abundant eosinophils (Th2 allergic inflammation), not neutrophils.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Statement D is CORRECT: The presence of bilateral sinonasal polyps is an absolute, mandatory major diagnostic criterion of Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (Bent & Kuhn criterion #2).

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize bilateral nasal polyposis as a mandatory clinical diagnostic criterion for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis.

questions.question:
A high-resolution coronal computed tomography (CT) scan of the paranasal sinuses at the level of the osteomeatal complex is displayed for review. A red arrow points directly to the paper-thin bony partition separating the ethmoid air cells from the intraorbital cone.

The structure indicated by the red arrow represents the:

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Coronal CT Scan: The red arrow points to the thin vertical bony plate of the medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone) directly separating the anterior ethmoidal air cells from the orbit.
questions.explanation:
The red arrow indicates the lamina papyracea (os planum), which is the paper-thin orbital plate of the ethmoid bone forming the vast majority of the medial orbital wall.

Surgical and Pathological Significance:
1. In functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), the lamina papyracea is the critical lateral boundary during anterior and posterior ethmoidectomy. Accidental surgical violation leads to intraorbital fat herniation, injury to the medial rectus muscle (causing diplopia), or transection of the anterior ethmoidal artery with retrobulbar hematoma.

2. In acute ethmoiditis, its thinness permits rapid extension of infection into the orbit, causing subperiosteal abscess and orbital cellulitis.

High-Yield: FESS Surgical Landmarks: Lamina papyracea = Lateral limit of ethmoidectomy (protect the orbit!). Skull base / fovea ethmoidalis = Superior limit (protect the brain/CSF!). Middle turbinate = Medial landmark (never resect unnecessarily; attachment stabilizes skull base).

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: If orbital fat is visualized during ethmoidectomy (floats in water test), the lamina papyracea has been violated! Never apply suction or blakesley forceps to orbital fat—it can avulse the medial rectus muscle!

optionExplanations.A: Correct: The red arrow indicates the lamina papyracea (os planum), which is the paper-thin orbital plate of the ethmoid bone forming the vast majority of the medial orbital wall.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: The uncinate process is the sickle-shaped bone of the lateral nasal wall resected during uncinectomy to expose the ethmoid infundibulum.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: The middle turbinate is the medial landmark attached superiorly to the cribriform plate and skull base.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: The cribriform plate forms the horizontal roof of the nasal cavity.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the lamina papyracea as the paper-thin medial orbital wall on coronal paranasal sinus CT.

questions.question:
Referring to the high-resolution coronal paranasal sinus CT scan, a pneumatized air cell located along the medial orbital floor immediately superior to the maxillary sinus natural ostium is indicated by an emoji pointer.

The anatomical structure indicated by the emoji represents a:

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Coronal CT Scan: Displays an infraorbital ethmoid cell (Haller cell) extending along the medial orbital floor, narrowing the ethmoid infundibulum and the natural ostium of the maxillary sinus.
questions.explanation:
The structure indicated is a Haller cell (also termed an infraorbital ethmoid cell).

Anatomy & Clinical Significance: A Haller cell is an ethmoid air cell that pneumatizes inferiorly along the medial orbital floor, projecting below the ethmoid bulla into the superior aspect of the maxillary sinus ostium or ethmoid infundibulum. When enlarged or inflamed, a Haller cell can significantly narrow or completely obstruct the ethmoid infundibulum and maxillary sinus ostium, predisposing the patient to recurrent or chronic ipsilateral maxillary sinusitis. During FESS, failure to identify and uncuff an obstructive Haller cell is a leading cause of persistent maxillary sinus disease.

High-Yield: High-Yield Sinus Anatomical Variants: Haller cell = Infraorbital ethmoid cell; narrows maxillary ostium/infundibulum. Onodi cell = Posterior ethmoid cell intimate with the Optic Nerve (risk of blindness during surgery!). Agger nasi cell = Anterior-most ethmoid cell; narrows frontal recess. Concha bullosa = Pneumatized middle turbinate.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Do not confuse Haller cell (floor of orbit / maxillary ostium) with Onodi cell (posterior ethmoid / optic nerve).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: The structure indicated is a Haller cell (also termed an infraorbital ethmoid cell).
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: An Onodi cell (sphenoethmoidal cell) is a posterior ethmoid cell that pneumatizes superolaterally to the sphenoid sinus, surrounding the optic nerve or internal carotid artery.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: A concha bullosa is pneumatization of the middle turbinate body itself.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: An Agger nasi cell is the most anterior ethmoid cell, situated anterior and superior to the insertion of the middle turbinate near the frontal recess.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a Haller cell (infraorbital ethmoid cell) on coronal CT as a pneumatized air cell on the orbital floor that can obstruct the maxillary sinus ostium.

questions.question:
An axial bone-window CT scan of the skull base demonstrates an isolated, unilateral opacification of the sphenoid sinus containing central punctate calcifications, sparing all anterior ethmoid, frontal, and maxillary sinuses. Biopsy confirms a non-invasive fungal ball.

Which of the following statements regarding sinonasal fungal balls (mycetomas) is correct?

Clinical / Radiological Finding: Axial CT Scan: Shows isolated, unilateral opacification of the left sphenoid sinus with heavy central hyperdensity and sclerosis of the sphenoid wall without bony erosion.

options.B: The maxillary sinus is the most commonly involved sinus overall

questions.explanation:
Statement B is CORRECT: Overall, the maxillary sinus is by far the single most common anatomical location for a sinonasal fungal ball (accounting for approximately 70–80% of all cases), followed second by the sphenoid sinus (~15–20%).

Correction of Incorrect Options:
• Option A is FALSE: Sinonasal fungal balls occur almost exclusively in immunocompetent hosts (often elderly females). Immunocompromised patients develop acute invasive fungal sinusitis.
• Option C is FALSE: Fungal balls are isolated non-atopic masses that are NOT associated with diffuse nasal polyposis (nasal polyps are typical of AFRS).
• Option D is FALSE: Fungal balls are completely non-invasive and do not invade the orbit or intracranial cavity.

High-Yield: Fungal Sinus Disease Quick Rule: Fungal Ball = Maxillary (75%) > Sphenoid (20%), non-invasive, immunocompetent, central calcification, no polyps. Acute Invasive = Angioinvasive, DKA/neutropenia, high mortality. AFRS = Young, atopic, pansinusitis, polyps, double-density.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Although the CT presented shows a SPHENOID fungal ball, the question asks about fungal balls overall: the MAXILLARY sinus is the most common site!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: Fungal balls occur in immunocompetent patients; invasive disease occurs in immunocompromised hosts.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: Statement B is CORRECT: Overall, the maxillary sinus is by far the single most common anatomical location for a sinonasal fungal ball (accounting for approximately 70–80% of all cases), followed second by the sphenoid sinus (~15–20%).
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect: Diffuse nasal polyposis is characteristic of Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS), not a fungal ball.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: Orbital invasion is seen in acute invasive fungal sinusitis, not a benign fungal ball.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the maxillary sinus as the most common anatomical site for sinonasal fungal balls overall.

questions.question:
Referring to the axial computed tomography scan displaying isolated unilateral sinus opacification at the center of the skull base, situated immediately anterior to the clivus and bounded laterally by the internal carotid arteries:

Which paranasal sinus is involved in this patient's scan?
questions.explanation:
The axial CT scan clearly localizes the pathology to the sphenoid sinus.

Anatomical Landmarks on Axial CT: The sphenoid sinus is situated within the body of the sphenoid bone at the central skull base. It lies directly below the sella turcica, anterior to the basilar clivus and brainstem, and medial to the cavernous sinus and internal carotid canal. Isolated sphenoid sinus disease often presents deceptively with an intractable vertex or deep retro-orbital headache.

High-Yield: Isolated Sphenoid Sinus Opacification: Presenting symptom is almost always severe, deep, refractory headache (vertex or retro-orbital). Differential diagnosis includes fungal ball, mucocele, inverted papilloma, and sphenoid encephaloceles. Endoscopic sphenoidotomy is definitive.

Exam Trap / Do Not Miss: Sphenoid sinus lesions can compress the optic nerve (superiorly) or carotid artery (laterally). Any isolated sphenoid mass requires high-resolution CT and MRI before biopsy.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: The anterior ethmoidal air cells are located anteriorly between the orbits.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect: The posterior ethmoid air cells lie immediately anterior to the sphenoid face.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: The axial CT scan clearly localizes the pathology to the sphenoid sinus.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect: The maxillary sinuses are large paired pyramidal cavities within the cheekbones lateral to the nasal cavity.

questions.educationalObjective: Localize the sphenoid sinus at the central skull base on axial CT imaging.

questions.question:
